questions.q: In which state and year did the Navnirman Andolan begin, and what was its immediate trigger?
questions.a: The Navnirman Andolan began in Gujarat in 1974, triggered by a steep hike in hostel mess fees at L.D. College of Engineering, Ahmedabad. A wrong answer (e.g., "Bihar, 1975" or "triggered by railway strike") reveals the student conflates the two movements or misses the student-origin character of Navnirman.

questions.q: Why did Jayaprakash Narayan, a veteran Gandhian, come out of retirement to lead the JP Movement in 1974?
questions.a: JP was moved by the widespread corruption, unemployment, and the government's authoritarian drift after the 1971 victory; he saw the Bihar student protests as a spark for a nationwide "Total Revolution" to morally regenerate politics. A wrong answer (e.g., "he wanted to become Prime Minister" or "he was invited by Indira Gandhi") shows the student misunderstands JP's non-partisan, moral-authority leadership and his critique of concentrated power.

questions.q: A group of students in a state university today protests a 50% tuition fee increase, organizes a peaceful gherao of the registrar, and gets support from opposition parties. Using the Navnirman Andolan as a framework, identify two similarities and one key difference in the political context.
questions.a: Similarities: (1) Student-led initiative over economic grievance, (2) escalation to broader civil society support. Difference: In 1974, the Congress government had no institutionalized grievance redressal mechanisms and faced a unified opposition; today, universities have statutory fee committees and the anti-defection law limits party-switching. A wrong answer that misses the "broader civil society escalation" or cites "social media" as a 1974 factor reveals anachronistic reasoning.

questions.q: Compare the leadership structure and ideological scope of the JP Movement and the Navnirman Andolan.
questions.a: Navnirman was decentralized, led by student action committees with no single charismatic figure, focused on corruption and fees. JP Movement had a clear national leader (Jayaprakash Narayan), articulated a comprehensive "Total Revolution" ideology (political, economic, social, cultural, educational), and explicitly sought to dissolve the Bihar assembly. A wrong answer claiming both were "party-led" or "violent" ignores their non-partisan, largely non-violent character — a frequent board-exam trap.

questions.q: Evaluate the argument: "The JP Movement and Navnirman Andolan justified the imposition of Emergency because they created law-and-order breakdown."
questions.a: The argument is flawed: both movements were overwhelmingly non-violent and demanded accountability, not regime overthrow; the government used them as a pretext, but the immediate trigger was the Allahabad High Court verdict unseating Indira Gandhi. A student who agrees without mentioning the court verdict or the non-violent nature fails to distinguish between "internal disturbance" (Article 352 ground) and legitimate democratic dissent — a critical distinction for board and competitive exams.

questions.q: Design a poster slogan for a modern "Total Revolution" campaign against electoral corruption, using JP's seven-point programme as inspiration. Explain each element in one line.
questions.a: Example slogan: "Clean Money, Clean Politics — Total Revolution 2.0". Elements: (1) State funding of elections — ends corporate capture, (2) Right to Recall — enforces accountability, (3) Ban on criminal candidates — upholds probity, (4) Transparent party funding — ends black money, (5) Inner-party democracy — decentralizes power, (6) Citizen audit of MPs — participatory vigilance, (7) Electoral reform commission — institutionalizes integrity. A poor answer lists vague slogans without linking to JP's specific seven points, showing lack of textual engagement.
